title: Gleason: extremally disconnected equals projective
statement:
Let $S$ be a compact Hausdorff space. The following are equivalent.

1. $S$ is extremally disconnected: for every open $U\subset S$, the closure
   $\overline U$ is open.
2. $S$ is projective for continuous surjections of compact Hausdorff spaces: for every
   continuous surjection $p\colon X\to Y$ of compact Hausdorff spaces and every continuous
   $f\colon S\to Y$ there is a continuous $g\colon S\to X$ with $p\circ g=f$.
3. Every continuous surjection $q\colon P\to S$ from a compact Hausdorff space $P$ has a
   continuous section.

Moreover an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space is totally disconnected, hence
profinite.

proof.text: *2 $\Rightarrow$ 3.* Apply the lifting property to $p=q$ and $f=\mathrm{id}_S$. Its lift $\sigma:S\to P$ is continuous and satisfies $q\circ\sigma=\mathrm{id}_S$, which is precisely a section.

source.place: Tag 08YN, proof, implication (3) to (2) in the source numbering.

proof.text: *3 $\Rightarrow$ 2, admissibility of the pullback.* Given $p:X\to Y$ and $f:S\to Y$ as in 2, set $P=\{(s,x)\in S\times X:f(s)=p(x)\}$ with the subspace topology. The product $S\times X$ is quasi-compact by [lem-weil-pbc-tychonoff-product-quasi-compact] with a two-element index set. It is Hausdorff: distinct pairs differ in a coordinate, whose disjoint neighbourhoods pull back to disjoint product neighbourhoods. The subset $P$ is closed: if $f(s)\ne p(x)$, disjoint open neighbourhoods of these points in $Y$ pull back to a product neighbourhood of $(s,x)$ avoiding $P$. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-closed-in-quasi-compact] makes $P$ quasi-compact, and intersecting disjoint ambient neighbourhoods with $P$ makes it Hausdorff.

source.place: Tag 08YN, proof, pullback argument; Tag 08ZU, theorem-tychonov; Tag 005C, lemma-closed-in-quasi-compact.

proof.text: *3 $\Rightarrow$ 2, lift.* The projection $q:P\to S$ is continuous, and it is surjective because for any $s$ surjectivity of $p$ supplies $x$ with $p(x)=f(s)$. Apply 3 to this compact Hausdorff source to obtain a continuous section $\sigma$. The second projection gives $g=\mathrm{pr}_X\circ\sigma$; for each $s$, membership $\sigma(s)\in P$ gives $p(g(s))=f(q(\sigma(s)))=f(s)$.

source.place: Tag 08YN, proof, pullback argument, with its omitted details supplied.

proof.text: *3 $\Rightarrow$ 1, the test surjection.* For open $U\subset S$, put $A=\overline U$ and $B=S\setminus U$ with their subspace topologies. Both are closed in $S$, hence quasi-compact by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-in-quasi-compact], and Hausdorff by restriction of disjoint neighbourhoods in $S$. Give $P=A\sqcup B$ the disjoint union topology. It is quasi-compact: restrict an open covering to each summand, take finite subcoverings there, and unite the two finite families. It is Hausdorff by separation within a summand and by the disjoint open summands for points in different summands. The two inclusions define a continuous surjection $q:P\to S$, since $A\cup B=S$. By 3 it has a continuous section $\sigma$.

source.place: Tag 08YN, proof, last paragraph: the surjection from the disjoint union of the closure and complement.

proof.text: *3 $\Rightarrow$ 1, identify the clopen inverse image.* The first summand of $P$ is clopen, so $C=\sigma^{-1}(A\text{ in the first summand})$ is clopen in $S$. For $s\in U$, its fibre under $q$ has no point in the second summand, hence $U\subset C$. Closedness gives $\overline U\subset C$. Conversely $s\in C$ implies $s=q(\sigma(s))\in A=\overline U$. Thus $C=\overline U$, so $\overline U$ is open.

source.place: Tag 08YN, proof, last paragraph, equality of the inverse image with the closure expanded.

proof.text: *1 $\Rightarrow$ 3, chain intersections.* Fix a continuous surjection $q:P\to S$ with $P$ compact Hausdorff and assume 1. Let $\mathcal E$ be the set of closed subsets $E\subseteq P$ with $q(E)=S$; it contains $P$. For a nonempty inclusion chain $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal E$ put $E_{\mathcal C}=\bigcap_{E\in\mathcal C}E$, a closed subset of $P$. Fix $s\in S$. The fibre $q^{-1}(\{s\})$ is closed: a singleton is closed in a Hausdorff space, since every other point has an open neighbourhood avoiding it; now use continuity. The closed sets $E\cap q^{-1}(\{s\})$ are nonempty and have nonempty finite intersections, since a finite nonempty subchain has a smallest member. If their total intersection were empty, their open complements in $P$ would cover $P$, and a finite subcover would contradict that finite-intersection property. (The empty finite subfamily also has nonempty intersection $P$, because $s$ has a preimage.) Thus $s\in q(E_{\mathcal C})$, so $E_{\mathcal C}\in\mathcal E$. For the empty chain use the lower bound $P$.

source.place: Tag 08YM, lemma-find-compact-subset, chain/fibre argument; the finite-intersection fact is proved directly by the open-cover definition of compactness.

proof.text: *Minimal closed source.* To use [lem-weil-pbc-zorn-lemma] in its stated upper-bound form, apply it to $\mathcal O=\{P\setminus E:E\in\mathcal E\}\subseteq\mathcal P(P)$. Complementation turns a chain in $\mathcal O$ into a chain in $\mathcal E$. Step 6 makes the complement of its intersection an upper bound in $\mathcal O$; for the empty chain the upper bound is $\varnothing=P\setminus P$. Hence Zorn gives a maximal $O_0\in\mathcal O$. Set $P_0=P\setminus O_0$. It is closed, maps onto $S$, and is minimal among closed subsets of $P$ mapping onto $S$. It is compact by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-in-quasi-compact] and Hausdorff by restricting separating neighbourhoods in $P$. Write $q_0=q|_{P_0}$. A closed subset $F$ of $P_0$ is closed in $P$, since $P_0$ is closed; consequently no proper closed $F\subset P_0$ maps onto $S$.

source.place: Tag 08YM, lemma-find-compact-subset, Zorn argument; complement duality supplies the upper-bound form of the existing Mathlib leaf.

proof.text:
*The restricted map is closed.* For any closed $F\subseteq P_0$, [lem-weil-pbc-closed-in-quasi-compact] makes $F$ compact. If $s
otin q_0(F)$, choose for each $x\in F$ disjoint open neighbourhoods $U_x
i q_0(x)$ and $N_x
i s$ in $S$. The sets $F\cap q_0^{-1}(U_x)$ cover $F$, so finitely many suffice. The intersection of the corresponding $N_x$ is an open neighbourhood of $s$ avoiding $q_0(F)$. For $F=\varnothing$ take that neighbourhood to be $S$. Thus $q_0(F)$ is closed. This proves closedness directly from compactness and Hausdorff separation, rather than importing an unrecorded closed-map theorem.

source.place: Tag 08YL, lemma-isomorphism, closedness input; Tag 08YD, lemma-closed-map. The elementary finite-subcover proof of closedness is supplied here.

proof.text: *The opens $V^*$.* For each open $V\subseteq P_0$ set $V^*=S\setminus q_0(P_0\setminus V)$. Step 8 shows $V^*$ is open. Every fibre of $q_0$ is nonempty, and a point lies in $V^*$ exactly when its whole fibre lies in $V$; in particular $V^*\subseteq q_0(V)$. If $V\ne\varnothing$, then $P_0\setminus V$ is proper closed, so minimality from Step 7 makes $V^*$ nonempty. If $V\subseteq W$ then $V^*\subseteq W^*$ by the same fibre description.

source.place: Tag 08YJ, lemma-image-open-technical; the definition and elementary properties of V-star are those of the current blueprint, paragraph following the minimal-source construction.

proof.text: *Density at an image point.* If $a\in A\subseteq P_0$ with $A$ open and $s=q_0(a)$, then $s\in\overline{A^*}$. Indeed for any open neighbourhood $N$ of $s$, the set $V=A\cap q_0^{-1}(N)$ is nonempty open, since it contains $a$. Step 9 gives $\varnothing\ne V^*\subseteq A^*$ and $V^*\subseteq q_0(V)\subseteq N$. Thus every such $N$ meets $A^*$, which is precisely membership in its closure.

source.place: Tag 08YJ, lemma-image-open-technical, neighbourhood argument, in the V-star notation of the current blueprint.

proof.text:
*Injectivity from extremal disconnectedness.* Suppose $a
e b$ in $P_0$ with $q_0(a)=q_0(b)=s$. Hausdorffness of $P_0$ gives disjoint open neighbourhoods $A
i a$, $B
i b$. Their opens $A^*$ and $B^*$ are disjoint: a common point would have a nonempty fibre contained in $A\cap B=\varnothing$. Step 10 gives $s\in\overline{A^*}\cap\overline{B^*}$. Condition 1 makes $\overline{A^*}$ open, and this open neighbourhood of $s\in\overline{B^*}$ must meet $B^*$. But an open set $B^*$ disjoint from $A^*$ is disjoint from $\overline{A^*}$, because any point of their intersection would have the neighbourhood $B^*$ meeting $A^*$. This contradiction proves $q_0$ injective.

source.place: Tags 08YK, lemma-intersection-empty, and 08YL, lemma-isomorphism, injectivity argument. The disjoint-open/closure argument is written out, as in the current blueprint.

proof.text: *The section.* Now $q_0:P_0\to S$ is a continuous bijection, with compact source and Hausdorff target. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-compact-hausdorff-bijection] with its ambient spaces $P,S$ and subsets $P_0,S$: $q_0$ is a homeomorphism. Its inverse composed with the continuous subspace inclusion $P_0\hookrightarrow P$ is a continuous section of $q$, since $q\circ(P_0\hookrightarrow P)\circ q_0^{-1}=q_0\circ q_0^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_S$. This proves 3; together with Steps 1–5 it proves all three equivalences.

source.place: Tag 08YN, proposition-projective-in-category-hausdorff-qc, extremally disconnected implies sections, via Tags 08YM and 08YL; Tag 08YE, lemma-bijective-map.

proof.text:
*Total disconnectedness.* Assume 1. If $x
e y$, choose disjoint open neighbourhoods $U
i x$ and $V
i y$ by Hausdorffness. The closure $\overline U$ is clopen and contains $x$. It misses $y$, because the open neighbourhood $V$ avoids $U$. Any connected subset containing both $x$ and $y$ would then be separated into its nonempty intersections with $\overline U$ and its complement. Hence every connected subset has at most one point, which is total disconnectedness.

source.place: Tag 08YI, paragraph after definition-extremally-disconnected; the separating-clopen argument of the blueprint, final paragraph.

proof.text: *Profinite realization, including the empty space.* If $S=\varnothing$, it is the inverse limit of the diagram consisting of the empty finite discrete space. Assume now that $S\ne\varnothing$. Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of finite partitions of $S$ into nonempty clopen subsets. It contains $\{S\}$. Give it an arrow $\mathcal Q'\to\mathcal Q$ when $\mathcal Q'$ refines $\mathcal Q$, and send each block of $\mathcal Q'$ to its unique containing block of $\mathcal Q$. Nonempty intersections of blocks give common refinements; thus this is a cofiltered inverse system of finite discrete block sets. The map $h:S\to L=\varprojlim_{\mathcal Q\in\mathcal P}\mathcal Q$ sends a point to its block. It is continuous: the inverse image of a basic product neighbourhood restricted to $L$ is a finite intersection of unions of clopen blocks, hence open. Step 13 separates distinct points by clopens, and the partition into such a clopen and its complement separates their images, so $h$ is injective. For a compatible family $(C_{\mathcal Q})_{\mathcal Q}\in L$ and finitely many partitions $\mathcal Q_1,\ldots,\mathcal Q_n$, choose a common refinement $\mathcal R$. Compatibility gives $\varnothing\ne C_{\mathcal R}\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^n C_{\mathcal Q_i}$. Thus these selected closed blocks have the finite intersection property. If their total intersection were empty, their open complements would cover $S$; a finite subcover would contradict the displayed nonempty finite intersection. Any point in the total intersection maps to the given family, proving surjectivity. Distinct points of $L$, as a subspace of a product of finite discrete spaces, differ in a coordinate and have disjoint coordinate neighbourhoods, so $L$ is Hausdorff. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-compact-hausdorff-bijection] to $h$ (taking both subsets there to be the entire spaces): it is a homeomorphism. Thus $S$ is profinite in the inverse-limit definition.

source.place: Tag 08ZY, lemma-profinite, proof of (2) implies (1); Tag 08YE, lemma-bijective-map. The clopen separation needed in that proof is established in Step 13.
